# Kuruṅgamigajātaka (Ja 21)

**ID:** Ja 21
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Kuruṅgamigajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Antelope
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja21
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Kuruṅgamigajātaka* (Ja 21) is the opening story of the Sīlavagga in the single-verse section (*Ekanipāta*) of the Pali Jātaka collection [Fausböll 1877]. Its canonical verse begins with the phrase *Ñātam etaṁ kuruṅgassa* ("The antelope knows well") [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877]. According to the nidāna, the Buddha related the tale while residing at the Bamboo Grove (Veḷuvana) near Rājagaha in connection with Devadatta's persistent attempts to assassinate him—specifically recalling how Devadatta hired bowmen, rolled down a rock, and let loose the rogue elephant Dhanapālaka [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877]. Declaring that Devadatta had likewise attempted and failed to kill him in bygone times, the Buddha related the story of the past and identified the characters at the conclusion: the treacherous hunter was Devadatta in a former birth, whereas the Bodhisatta was the clever antelope (*kuruṅgamiga*) who outwitted him [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877].

Artistic representations of the Bodhisatta as the deer Kuruṅgamiga are attested on the gateway railings of Sāñcī Stūpa 1 [Karlsson 1999]. In the epigraphy and temple labels of Pagan-period Burma, the Jātaka title is attested across various monuments (such as the Ananda, Hpetleik, and Gubyaukgyi temples) under spelling variants including *Kurungāmiga*, *Kuruṅkamika*, *Gurungmiga*, and *Gurungāmika* [WinThanTun 2002].

SuttaCentral records translations of the Jātaka in four modern languages, including an English translation by Bhikkhu Sujato [SuttaCentral]. No Pali-internal text reuse or cross-language parallels with Chinese, Sanskrit, or Tibetan corpora are recorded in the DharmaNexus database [DharmaNexus].
